Exact ordered producer-consumer Go race/correctness validation

claims.text: The preserved Question asks for a producer-consumer 1:2 program that outputs 1-100 in order. The surrounding note is a Go-backend interview and the tagged entities include producer-consumer/channel; the notation itself does not define a function signature or spell out the meaning of 1:2.

Go channels are the communication mechanism selected by the surrounding Go context; ordered channel communication does not by itself serialize post-receive side effects performed by multiple independently scheduled consumers, so final ordered visibility is made a single-coordinator responsibility.
The exact candidate with two consumers returns the sequence 1..100 on every repeated race-enabled test run and across concurrent independent invocations.
The producer owns jobs closure; a WaitGroup-backed closer closes results only after all consumers exit, and the single coordinator owns pending/next state.

validation.command: extract exact Go candidate; gofmt; go test -race -count=5 ./...

findings: The answer keeps the only preserved requirement—producer/consumer 1:2 with ordered 1-100 output—separate from the candidate API contract and explicitly marks the 1-producer/2-consumer reading as an adopted interpretation.
Using Go is grounded in the surrounding Go-backend note and channel tag, not presented as wording contained in the Question itself.
The design correctly separates concurrent processing from ordered visible output; workers never own final printing/order state.
The exact candidate passes repeated two-consumer ordering tests under the race detector and independent concurrent invocations.
Channel closure ownership is fail-safe: producer closes jobs; results closes only after every consumer exits.
The answer explicitly rejects unsupported claims about worker fairness, distributed exactly-once, and fabricated production metrics.
